stem: Groundwork: Which choice covers the whole passage, not just one sentence of it?
stimulus: Many cities are replacing parking spaces with small public seating areas. In one riverside neighborhood, planners converted twelve curbside spaces into benches and planters. Within a year, nearby cafés reported more customers, and residents said the street felt safer at night. The project suggests that giving up a few parking spaces can make a street more useful to the people who walk along it.
choices: Nearby cafés gained customers after twelve parking spaces were removed.
Turning some parking into seating can make a street more useful to people.
Cities should remove all their parking to make streets safer at night.
Residents objected when planners replaced parking with benches and planters.
explanation: The first sentence names a trend, the middle sentences give one example, and the last sentence says what the example shows. Choice B is the only one that covers all of that: some parking becomes seating, and the street works better for people. This scope check (does the choice cover every sentence?) is the first step on every SAT main-idea question about an informational passage.

A.why: This is true, but it comes from one sentence in the middle. You picked a correct detail that is only part of the point. The passage uses the cafés as evidence for a larger claim.

C.why: The passage talks about giving up 'a few' spaces in one neighborhood. It never says cities should remove all parking. You let the topic grow into a claim the passage never makes.

D.why: The passage reports good results: more customers, and a street that felt safer. It mentions no objections. Go back to the passage before you accept a choice.

stem: Groundwork: Which choice covers the whole passage, not just one sentence of it?
stimulus: Woodcut printing is often thought of as a crude method suited only to bold, simple images. However, some eighteenth-century Japanese printers used it to produce remarkably subtle work. By carving a separate block for each color and aligning the paper with small notches, they layered as many as twenty colors into a single print with soft, precise shading.
choices: Some printers carved small notches into their blocks to help align the paper.
Woodcut is a crude method that is best suited to bold and simple images.
Woodcut printing, often seen as crude, could produce very subtle images.
Japanese woodcuts were the most technically advanced prints ever made.
explanation: The passage opens with a common view and then turns at 'However.' What comes after the turn is what the author believes: woodcut could be subtle. The last sentence explains how that was done. Choice C covers the view, the correction, and the evidence. The SAT often builds main-idea passages around a 'However' turn, and this habit helps with those.

A.why: The notches are a real detail, but they are only one part of how the printers worked. You picked an accurate piece of the final sentence instead of the point it supports.

B.why: This is the view the passage sets up only to correct. You stopped reading before 'However,' which is the word that tells you the author disagrees.

D.why: The passage says some printers did remarkably subtle work. It never compares them with every print ever made. 'Most advanced ever' is a much bigger claim than the text supports.

stem: Groundwork: Which choice covers the whole passage, not just one sentence of it?
stimulus: Medieval music manuscripts rarely record how fast a piece should be sung, so some musicologists look to other kinds of evidence. One researcher noticed that a monastery's daily schedule set aside only about ten minutes for a certain chant. If the monks kept to that schedule, the chant was likely sung much faster than it is usually performed today.
choices: A monastery's daily schedule set aside about ten minutes for one chant.
Medieval manuscripts give exact singing speeds for most of their chants.
Modern singers perform every medieval chant far more slowly than they should.
A monastery schedule points to one chant once being sung faster than today.
explanation: The passage goes from a problem (no tempo markings) to a clue (the schedule) to a careful conclusion about one chant ('if,' 'likely'). Choice D covers all three and makes the claim no stronger than the text does. Matching a choice's strength to hedge words like 'likely' is something you will need on real main-idea questions.

A.why: The passage does say this, but it is the clue and not the conclusion. You picked the most vivid fact, the ten minutes, instead of what the passage uses that fact to show.

B.why: The first sentence says manuscripts 'rarely record' speed. This choice says the opposite.

C.why: The passage is about one chant, and it hedges with 'if' and 'likely.' This choice covers every chant and sounds certain. It claims far more than the evidence allows.

stem: Groundwork: Which choice covers the whole passage, not just one sentence of it?
stimulus: Engineers inspecting an old stone bridge found that its arches had shifted only a few millimeters in a century. Its foundations rested on bedrock rather than soft clay. Its builders had also left channels that let floodwater pass beneath the road instead of pushing against it. Together, these features explain why the bridge has outlasted many newer ones nearby.
choices: Several features of its design explain why the old bridge has lasted so long.
The bridge's foundations were built on bedrock rather than on soft clay.
Floodwater has slowly weakened the arches of the old stone bridge over time.
Stone bridges always last longer than bridges made from newer materials.
explanation: The middle sentences list separate facts, and the last sentence ('Together...') combines them into one conclusion. Choice A is that conclusion. When a passage ends by adding up its details, the main idea is usually the sum and not any single item. You will see this pattern on SAT main-idea questions.

B.why: This is accurate, but it is one of the features, not the point they add up to. You chose a single correct sentence when the passage is doing more than that.

C.why: The passage says the channels let floodwater pass beneath the bridge, and that the arches barely moved. It does not say the arches were weakened.

D.why: The passage is about one bridge and the newer bridges near it. 'Always' and 'stone bridges' in general go well beyond what it says.
